newsitem.title: CHINA: China says progress seen in Korea peace talks.
newsitem.headline: China says progress seen in Korea peace talks.

text.p: China on Tuesday reported an advance in bringing Seoul, Pyongyang, Washington and Beijing together for talks on securing lasting peace on the Korean peninsula.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said: "We think it can be said that consultations involving all sides on holding four-way talks on the Korean peninsula have made progress." Shen did not elaborate at a news briefing.
"The Chinese side is willing to play a constructive role for peace and stability in the Korean peninsula," Shen said.

China's President Jiang Zemin told visiting South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-hwa in Beijing on Tuesday that China attached importance to its relations with South Korea, the Xinhua news agency said.
Beijing would push for the long-term development of friendly Sino-Korean ties, Jiang said.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen told Yoo on Monday that China wanted to join the talks on Korean peace, but on certain conditions.
China insists that rivals North and South Korea must first narrow their differences.
Famine-hit North Korea has requested massive food assistance as a condition for joining the proposed talks among the four countries -- the main combatants in the 1950-53 Korean war.
South Korea insists that large-scale food aid could only be discussed during the talks, and blamed Pyongyang's food crisis partly on its huge military spending.

Beijing's involvement in the four-way talks is seen as crucial by Seoul and Washington, which proposed the negotiations as a way of ending decades of military standoff along Korea's 38th parallel that divides North and South.
The Korean war was ended by a now-fraying armistice but the talks would be aimed at arranging a permanent treaty.
While the socialist solidarity between Beijing and Pyongyang has weakened in recent years, China is still seen as enjoying some influence over its isolated and hungry Stalinist neighbour.
